title: Deir el-Medina: Luxor's Overlooked Workers' Village
excerpt: Deir el-Medina is Luxor's overlooked workers' village: painted tombs of the people behind the Valley of the Kings, why it is worth an hour, and a shared tour from €60.
body_html:
Prices, timetables and visiting details are a November 2026 snapshot. Check the linked official pages and your departure’s current inclusions and terms before booking.

The quick answer

Yes, Deir el-Medina (also written Deir el Medina) is worth an hour of any Luxor trip. It is the walled village of the workmen who cut and painted the royal tombs: about 68 mudbrick houses, a few small tombs glowing with paint, and the ostraca, roughly 5,000 limestone and pottery notes that record the workers' daily lives. It is also the calmest stop on a busy West Bank day. Which tombs are open rotates, so treat any single tomb as a bonus rather than a promise.

UNESCO documents the temples and necropolis of ancient Thebes, including Luxor and its West Bank.

You have done the Valley of the Kings and the West Bank day has two stops left. One is Deir el-Medina, a walled mudbrick village where the people who built the royal tombs lived with their families. Many visitors rush it in fifteen minutes; it is the stop that makes the West Bank make sense: first the tombs, then their makers. Sawa Tours (sawa.tours), the Egypt shared-departure marketplace, lists the Grand West Bank tour that ends here; its founder has worked in Egyptian tourism since 1993.

What is Deir el-Medina? The village of the pharaohs' tomb-builders

Deir el-Medina was purpose-built for the crews who cut and painted the royal tombs of the Valley of the Kings and the Valley of the Queens. Egyptians called the village Set Maat, "the Place of Truth", and its people "Servants in the Place of Truth". The earliest datable remains go back to Thutmose I, and the village stayed occupied through the 18th, 19th and 20th Dynasties (about 1550 to 1080 BCE).

About 68 houses of around four rooms fit inside the enclosure wall, with daily life moving up to the roof. The workmen were state employees paid in rations, organised into two gangs under foremen, and they wrote constantly, so the villagers left one of the ancient world's best-documented communities.

What you'll see at Deir el-Medina: village, tombs and temple

Three rewards share the site: the village lanes, a handful of small painted tombs and a Ptolemaic temple. All three fit in an hour.

The Tomb of Sennedjem (TT1)

Sennedjem, a Servant in the Place of Truth who worked under Seti I and Ramesses II, was buried here with at least 20 people, family members among them, in a tomb found in January 1886. Its burial chamber, reached by a steep, narrow descent, is painted with Book of the Dead scenes on a warm yellow ground, among them Sennedjem and his wife Iyneferti working the fields of the afterlife. The finds were scattered: his coffin set stayed in Cairo, while objects from the tomb ended up in museums such as the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Visitor access to TT1 is not guaranteed in every season, so ask whether it is open on the day.

The other workers' tombs

Neighbouring craftsmen lie in similar chambers. Recent visitor reports describe the tombs of Inherkhau (TT359) and the group of Amennakht, Nebenmaat and Khaemteri (TT218 to 220) as open, with Pashedu (TT3) available on an extra ticket. These rooms hold some of the most colourful painting in Egypt. They open on rotation to protect the paint, so ask which are open that day.

The Temple of Hathor

By the entrance stands the small Ptolemaic temple of Hathor, goddess of love and joy, built on the site of an older shrine. In the Christian era it became a monastery, which gave the site its modern name: Deir el-Medina means "Monastery of the City" in Arabic.

Ostraca: the workmen's notes, sketches and strikes

Ostraca (the plural of ostracon) are limestone flakes and pottery shards the villagers used as notepaper, because papyrus was expensive. Around 5,000 were found in a well near the village, and they hold work rosters, receipts, hymns and sketches that rank among the liveliest art to survive from ancient Egypt. They even record a strike: when rations ran late under Ramesses III, the crews stopped work, an episode often described as the first recorded labour strike in history.

Deir el-Medina and the Tombs of the Nobles

The Tombs of the Nobles are the decorated private tombs of Theban officials, at Qurnet Murai beside the village and across the hillside at Sheikh Abd el-Qurna. Where royal tombs are full of underworld texts, nobles' tombs show daily life: farming, banquets, workshops. They carry separate tickets, with individual tombs listed at roughly EGP 120 to 200 (about €2 to €3.30) and cashless payment reported from the 2026 season. They are not on the Grand West Bank itinerary; Deir el-Medina stands in as the craftsmen-focused visit.

Visiting Deir el-Medina: timings, tickets and the shape of the day

Deir el-Medina works best as the late-afternoon stop it forms on a full West Bank day: the village is flat, exposed ground with little shade, and by then the heat is easing. On the Grand West Bank tour it gets its own slot near the day's end. The order of the day, as listed in November 2026:

  1. Hotel pickup in Luxor and the crossing to the West Bank.
  2. Valley of the Kings. Three royal tombs on the standard ticket (EGP 750, about €12.50); special tombs such as Tutankhamun's (EGP 700, about €11.70) are separate tickets.
  3. Valley of the Queens.
  4. Colossi of Memnon.
  5. Temple of Hatshepsut at Deir el-Bahari.
  6. Lunch at a local restaurant, included.
  7. Medinet Habu, Ramesses III's mortuary temple.
  8. Deir el-Medina, for about 50 minutes: village, workers' tombs and the temple of Hathor.
  9. Back at your hotel in the late afternoon.

The tour runs about nine hours and costs from €60 per person, as listed in November 2026, with entrance tickets, lunch, a licensed guide, transport and hotel pickup included. Special tombs, including Tutankhamun's and Nefertari's, are never included. The Tomb of Nefertari (QV66) in the Valley of the Queens has been reported closed for restoration since March 2024 with no reopening date announced, so do not plan around it. The Luxor in Depth full-day tour skips the village: pick the Grand West Bank if Deir el-Medina is the point.

Insider tips for Deir el-Medina

Five tips from our team:

  • Ask which tombs are open before you queue. The workers' tombs rotate for conservation, and the best painting may be in a name you have not heard of.
  • Hat for the lanes, steady shoes for the stairs. The village is flat and shadeless; the tombs drop steeply underground, so skip the stairs if enclosed spaces trouble you.
  • Look along the main street. It may once have been roofed against the sun, and you can still trace the layout of the lanes.
  • Link Medinet Habu to the strike. The tour reaches the village straight from Ramesses III's mortuary temple, the king under whom the crews struck over late rations. The story gains an address.
  • Bring a card. Ticket booths on the West Bank are reported to be moving to card-only payment, and photo rules inside tombs change, so ask at the booth rather than assume.

The verdict on Deir el-Medina

Deir el-Medina turns the West Bank's royal tombs into a human story: the people who dug and painted them lived in about 68 mudbrick houses, wrote on limestone chips and once struck over late rations. faq.a: Yes, for anyone curious how the Valley of the Kings came to be. It is the one place in Egypt where you can walk a complete ancient workers' village, enter small tombs painted by the community's own craftsmen and learn about the strike that is often called the first recorded in history. Give it 45 to 60 minutes.

faq.q: Which tombs can you enter at Deir el-Medina?
faq.a: It changes. The most famous is the Tomb of Sennedjem (TT1), found in January 1886, but it is not always open. Recent visitor reports mention Inherkhau (TT359) and the TT218 to 220 group as open, with Pashedu (TT3) on an extra ticket. Ask on the day. The nearby Tombs of the Nobles are separate tickets.

faq.q: How much time does Deir el-Medina need?
faq.a: Plan 45 to 60 minutes for the village lanes, one or two painted tombs and the temple of Hathor. The Grand West Bank tour allots about 50 minutes late in the day, which works well: by mid-afternoon the shadeless village is cooling and the morning crowds are long gone.

faq.q: Can you visit Deir el-Medina without a tour?
faq.a: Yes. Taxis cross from Luxor's East Bank in roughly half an hour, and entry is EGP 220 per foreign adult (as of November 2026), by card. The trade-off is context: the tombs and ostraca carry little signage, so a licensed Egyptologist guide changes what you get from the hour.

faq.a: Nothing is charged. A Sawa date confirms (the GoAhead) once four travellers have reserved it, and before that no money is taken. A date has until 7 days before the tour to reach four; if it does not, it is cancelled, you pay nothing, and Sawa suggests another date. Once confirmed, the day is not cancelled for low numbers: a traveller who misses a payment is excluded and the tour continues for the rest.
